sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.content: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) is a classic **string dynamic-programming** problem. A subsequence need not be contiguous — it only has to keep the original [[primary|relative order]].
items: Define **dp[i][j]** as the LCS length of the first i characters of textA and the first j of textB
When characters **match**, extend from the diagonal: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
When they **differ**, take the larger of up and left: max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
After filling the table, **trace back** from the bottom-right to recover the subsequence itself

sections.heading: Operation Complexity
sections.content: Every pair of characters from the two strings is evaluated once, so the whole 2D table must be filled.
items: **Time complexity**: [[warning|O(m × n)]], where m and n are the string lengths
**Space complexity**: [[warning|O(m × n)]] — the full DP table is kept for tracing back
Row 0 and column 0 represent the **empty string**, whose LCS length is always 0

sections.heading: What It Optimizes
sections.content: LCS is not just an exercise — it underpins many real tools.
items: **Rolling array**: if only the length is needed, space drops to [[success|O(min(m, n))]]; recovering the subsequence requires the full table
**Real uses**: file diffing, DNA sequence alignment
The same recurrence idea extends to other string DP problems such as **edit distance**
